name: Cosse Green
lede: Cosse Green is a moderate yellow green that Ridgway's 1912 dictionary and the 1955 ISCC-NBS circular both catalog, its name likely from the French *cosse* for a seed pod, though no source we checked confirms it.

sections.title: A pod-colored yellow-green
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 "Color Standards and Color Nomenclature" lists Cosse Green at #AAAE46, plate V, hue 29, tone i [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular repeats it in its "moderate yellow green" block, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary separately dates a first recorded use to 1905, seven years before Ridgway's own book [1]. *Cosse* is French for a pea pod or husk, a plausible source for the name, but none of the 29 books behind our concordance confirms the connection, so it stays undocumented here [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[olive-green]] and [[russet-green]], at A little further, at 8.5 units, is [[greenish-yellow|Greenish Yellow]], the plainer name for the same family [1]. The Munsell notation is 1.5GY 6.8/7.3, and the swatch sits with our [[yellow|yellow]] family, close enough to its green modifier to also sit near [[green|green]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 0.26% of 23,781 paintings, 62 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 51 [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.1% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 3.8 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as an accent, in 75% of its 51 appearances [2]. Georges Seurat is its most devoted painter, holding it in 4 of 41 works here, 6.4 times the baseline of the museums his paintings come from [2]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.1 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest match dates to 1500, by Hieronymus Bosch, 412 years before Ridgway recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
